cues.text: A Vow at Fourteen
Born in 1601 at Ri, in Normandy, John took a private vow of chastity at only fourteen years old.
After brilliant studies with the Jesuits at Caen, he entered the French Oratory founded by Cardinal Pierre de Bérulle in 1623.
There, he formed his spiritual life under Bérulle and his successor Charles de Condren, two leading figures of the French school of spirituality.
Heroic Ministry Amid Plague
Ordained a priest in 1625, John began his priestly life with striking courage, volunteering to nurse and minister to victims of a severe plague outbreak in his own diocese.
The work was so dangerous that he was obliged to live in isolation, in a barrel in an open field, to avoid infecting his own religious community.
A Renowned Missionary Preacher

John became one of the most celebrated popular mission preachers in seventeenth-century France, delivering some 110 parish missions over his lifetime across Normandy and beyond, including major preaching campaigns in Paris and at the royal court.
Contemporaries considered him the greatest missionary preacher France had produced since St. Vincent Ferrer , two centuries earlier.
Founding Refuges and Seminaries
In 1641, moved by the plight of women seeking to leave prostitution, John founded the Congregation of Our Lady of Charity of the Refuge to provide them shelter and support.
Two years later, with the encouragement of Cardinal Richelieu, he left the Oratory to found the Congregation of Jesus and Mary (the Eudists).
The congregation was dedicated to establishing seminaries for training diocesan priests, responding to the widespread lack of structured clerical formation in France at the time.
Pioneer of Devotion to the Sacred Hearts
John holds a distinctive place in Catholic devotional history as the first to compose a formal liturgical Mass and Office in honor of the Sacred Heart of Mary (1648).

He later composed one honoring the Sacred Heart of Jesus (1672), preceding by more than two decades the visions of St. Margaret Mary Alacoque that would later spread this devotion far more widely across the Church.
Legacy
John died at Caen in 1680, and was declared 'the author of the liturgical worship of the Sacred Hearts of Jesus and Mary' by Pope Leo XIII in 1903.
Canonized in 1925, his two religious foundations — the Eudists and the Sisters of Our Lady of Charity — continue their founder's twin commitments.

These include priestly formation and the rehabilitation of vulnerable women, while his devotional writings helped establish the Sacred Heart as one of the most widespread devotions in the modern Catholic Church.
